scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The manuscript provides a well-motivated architectural design addressing known domain shift challenges in remote sensing dense prediction. The experimental design is rigorous, evaluating multiple shift modalities (geographic, spectral, and cross-dataset) with comprehensive baselines, detailed ablation studies, and efficiency profiles.

reliability router that applies bounded spatial correction according to local prediction reliability. The
entire framework requires only source-domain supervision. Extensive experiments on the ISPRS,
LoveDA, and OpenEarthMap benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ASCoR across

domain generalization on three remote-sensing semantic

Table 7 distinguishes physically allocated task-specific
parameters from the subset that is active under the final
rank configuration. This distinction is necessary because
DynamicAdaptiveLoRAretainsmaximum-ranktensorsfor
flexibleallocationbutactivatesonlytheslicesselectedbythe
learned rank map.
The complete framework contains 1.721B resident pa-
rameters, of which 40.302M (2.341%) are task-specific.
Stage-wise optimization keeps the largest number of si-
multaneously trainable parameters to 27.715M, equivalent
to 1.61% of the complete model. Router learning updates
only 4,033 parameters, and the final forward computation
activates 30.865M task-specific parameters (1.793%). This
design concentrates task learning in a small set of param-
eters while retaining the pretrained representations of both
branches. The two SAM3 encoders account for most of the
total model size and inference cost.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported performance metrics directly support the claims: ASCoR achieves top average mIoU on ISPRS transfers (68.61%) and leads across all three LoveDA/OpenEarthMap shifts, with parameter counts and latency numbers showing PEFT efficiency (updating under 1.61% resident parameters during any stage).
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation covers nine directed domain shifts across ISPRS (Potsdam and Vaihingen), LoveDA (Urban and Rural), and OpenEarthMap benchmarks, comparing against established CNN/Transformer segmenters, UDA methods, and foundation-model adaptation baselines using standard class-wise IoU and mIoU. Ablations cleanly isolate the contributions of adaptive rank allocation, dense branch guidance, and router optimization objectives.

primary.limitations: The work relies on large foundation models (two frozen SAM3 encoders resulting in 1.72B total resident parameters), requiring significant compute resources for inference, and assumes access to pre-defined category text prompts.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, describing a three-stage sequential training procedure where TCSB adapts with Probe-Once Dynamic Adaptive LoRA, TSDB trains with complementary error-weighted loss on original and randomized views, and the reliability router learns bounded gate weights using source-domain utility and consistency objectives without modifying pretrained backbone weights.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript provides a well-motivated architectural design addressing known domain shift challenges in remote sensing dense prediction. The experimental design is rigorous, evaluating multiple shift modalities (geographic, spectral, and cross-dataset) with comprehensive baselines, detailed ablation studies, and efficiency profiles.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces ASCoR, an asymmetric dual-branch SAM3-based architecture for source-only domain generalization in remote sensing semantic segmentation, combining a text-conditioned semantic branch with adaptive low-rank allocation, a task-specific dense branch with complementary spatial supervision, and a lightweight reliability router for bounded spatial fusion.
